claim: MgtA is a specialized P-type ATPase believed to import Mg2+ into the cytoplasm.
source: The magnesium transporter A (MgtA) is a specialized P-type ATPase, believed to import Mg2+ into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of MgtA.

claim: In Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli, the PhoQ/PhoP two-component system regulates the transcription of mgtA gene by sensing Mg2+ concentrations in the periplasm.
source: In Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli, the virulence determining two-component system PhoQ/PhoP regulates the transcription of mgtA gene by sensing Mg2+ concentrations in the periplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MgtA is highly dependent on anionic phospholipids, particularly cardiolipin.
source: This study demonstrates, for the first time, that MgtA is highly dependent on anionic phospholipids and in particular, cardiolipin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: MgtA colocalizes with cardiolipin lipid domains in the membrane.
source: Colocalization studies confirm that MgtA is found in the cardiolipin lipid domains in the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 3A.

claim: The head group of cardiolipin plays a major role in activation of MgtA.
source: The head group of cardiolipin plays major role in activation of MgtA suggesting that cardiolipin may act as a Mg2+ chaperone for MgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing E. coli and bovine heart CL in Figure 2D.

claim: Cardiolipin may act as a Mg2+ chaperone for MgtA.
source: The head group of cardiolipin plays major role in activation of MgtA suggesting that cardiolipin may act as a Mg2+ chaperone for MgtA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings about cardiolipin activation.

claim: MgtA is highly sensitive to free Mg2+ (Mg2+free) levels in solution.
source: We further show that MgtA is highly sensitive to free Mg2+ (Mg2+free) levels in the solution.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: MgtA is activated when the Mg2+free concentration is reduced below 10 μM.
source: MgtA is activated when the Mg2+free concentration is reduced below 10 μM and is strongly inhibited above 1 mM, indicating that Mg2+free acts as product inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: MgtA is strongly inhibited above 1 mM Mg2+free.
source: MgtA is activated when the Mg2+free concentration is reduced below 10 μM and is strongly inhibited above 1 mM, indicating that Mg2+free acts as product inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Mg2+free acts as a product inhibitor of MgtA.
source: MgtA is activated when the Mg2+free concentration is reduced below 10 μM and is strongly inhibited above 1 mM, indicating that Mg2+free acts as product inhibitor.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the inhibition pattern observed at high Mg2+free concentrations.

claim: MgtA may act as both a sensor and a transporter of Mg2+.
source: Combined, our findings conclude that MgtA may act as a sensor as well as a transporter of Mg2+.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings about Mg2+ sensitivity and transport.

claim: Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation in biological systems.
source: Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation in biological systems and is an essential requirement for all living cells (Reinhart, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mg2+ is an essential requirement for all living cells.
source: Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation in biological systems and is an essential requirement for all living cells (Reinhart, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mg2+ has diverse biological roles, ranging from being an essential cofactor in ATP-mediated enzymatic reactions to being a signaling molecule that activates important virulence systems in bacteria.
source: Mg2+ has diverse biological roles, ranging from being an essential cofactor in ATP-mediated enzymatic reactions to being a signaling molecule that activates important virulence systems in bacteria (Groisman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Three classes of Mg2+ transporters have been identified in bacteria: CorA, MgtE and MgtA/MgtB.
source: Three classes of Mg2+ transporters have been identified in bacteria: CorA, MgtE and MgtA (magnesium transporter A)/MgtB.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: CorA transports Mg2+ under normal Mg2+ levels, whereas MgtA and MgtB transport Mg2+ when bacteria face low Mg2+ conditions.
source: Based on the Mg2+ transport studies, Snavely et al., proposed that CorA transports Mg2+ under normal Mg2+ levels, whereas MgtA and MgtB transport Mg2+ when bacteria faces low Mg2+ condition (Snavely et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Low Mg2+ levels in the periplasm activate the PhoQ/P system.
source: Later Garcia Vescovi et al., identified that the low Mg2+ levels in the periplasm activate the PhoQ/P system (Véscovi et al., 1996), which in turn induces the expression of genes essential for adapting the Mg2+ limiting environments (Monsieurs et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The PhoQ/P system induces the expression of genes essential for adapting to Mg2+ limiting environments.
source: Later Garcia Vescovi et al., identified that the low Mg2+ levels in the periplasm activate the PhoQ/P system (Véscovi et al., 1996), which in turn induces the expression of genes essential for adapting the Mg2+ limiting environments (Monsieurs et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: mgtA is one of the genes induced by the PhoQ/P system.
source: One of the genes was found to be mgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction following the discussion of PhoQ/P system.

claim: A Mg2+ sensing riboswitch at the 5' leader region activates the transcription of mgtA gene when the Mg2+ level in cytoplasm falls below a certain threshold.
source: In addition to PhoQ/P mediated activation, a Mg2+ sensing riboswitch at the 5' leader region was found to activate the transcription of mgtA gene when the Mg2+ level in cytoplasm falls below a certain threshold (Cromie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both intracellular and extracellular Mg2+ concentrations regulate transcription of the mgtA gene.
source: Therefore, both the intracellular and extracellular Mg2+ concentrations regulate transcription of the mgtA gene.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the PhoQ/P and riboswitch mechanisms.

claim: MgtA is believed to transport Mg2+ from the periplasm into the cytoplasm under Mg2+ depriving conditions.
source: Upon translation, MgtA is believed to transport Mg2+ from the periplasm into the cytoplasm under Mg2+ depriving conditions (Snavely et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Deletion of the mgtA gene affects the survival of S. typhimurium at higher temperatures.
source: It has been shown that deletion of the mgtA gene affects the survival of S. typhimurium at higher temperatures and also promotes lysis in Streptococcus pneumonia (O'Connor et al., 2009; Neef et al., 2011) .
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Deletion of the mgtA gene promotes lysis in Streptococcus pneumonia.
source: It has been shown that deletion of the mgtA gene affects the survival of S. typhimurium at higher temperatures and also promotes lysis in Streptococcus pneumonia (O'Connor et al., 2009; Neef et al., 2011) .
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MgtA belongs to the P3 subfamily of P-type ATPases.
source: MgtA belongs to the P3 subfamily of P-type ATPases (Palmgren and Axelsen, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The P3 family is subdivided into P3A and P3B.
source: The P3 family is subdivided into P3A and P3B.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The P3A family is dominated by H+-ATPases found in plants.
source: The P3A family is dominated by H+-ATPases found in plants (Palmgren, 2001), while P3B contains Mg2+ ATPases, found to be dominant amongst prokaryotes (Kühlbrandt, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: P3B contains Mg2+ ATPases, found to be dominant amongst prokaryotes.
source: The P3A family is dominated by H+-ATPases found in plants (Palmgren, 2001), while P3B contains Mg2+ ATPases, found to be dominant amongst prokaryotes (Kühlbrandt, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A close homolog of MgtA was reported in Petunia hybrida (PH1), which lacks the ability to induce a proton gradient.
source: Recently, a close homolog of MgtA was reported in Petunia hybrida (PH1), which lacks the ability to induce a proton gradient. PH1 was proposed to support the proton pumping performed by the P3A proton pump PH5, but evidence for magnesium transport was not established (Faraco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: PH1 was proposed to support the proton pumping performed by the P3A proton pump PH5, but evidence for magnesium transport was not established.
source: Recently, a close homolog of MgtA was reported in Petunia hybrida (PH1), which lacks the ability to induce a proton gradient. PH1 was proposed to support the proton pumping performed by the P3A proton pump PH5, but evidence for magnesium transport was not established (Faraco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: MgtA is found in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants.
source: In general, MgtA is found in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants (See also Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by phylogenetic tree data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2.

claim: MgtA has ten predicted transmembrane helices (TM), a nucleotide binding domain (N), a phosphorylation domain (P) and an actuator domain (A).
source: MgtA has ten predicted transmembrane helices (TM), a nucleotide binding domain (N), a phosphorylation domain (P) and an actuator domain (A) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Post-Albers cycle describes the transport mechanism of a P-type ATPase.
source: The Post-Albers cycle describes the transport mechanism of a P-type ATPase (Albers, 1967; Post et al., 1969).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: P-type ATPases alternate between the E1 and E2 states with different intermediate conformational states during the transport cycle.
source: During the transport cycle, P-type ATPases alternate between the E1 and E2 states with different intermediate conformational states (Palmgren and Nissen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The E1 state has high affinity and is open for ions binding from the cytoplasm.
source: The E1 state has high affinity and is open for ions binding from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the Post-Albers cycle description.

claim: Ion binding induces autophosphorylation by transferring the γ-phosphate from an ATP molecule to a conserved aspartate residue in the DKTGT consensus motif of the P domain forming the E1P state.
source: Ion binding induces autophosphorylation by transferring the γ-phosphate from an ATP molecule to a conserved aspartate residue in the DKTGT consensus motif of the P domain forming the E1P state (Lutsenko and Kaplan, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In E. coli MgtA (ecMgtA), the phosphorylated aspartate corresponds to Asp 373.
source: In E. coli MgtA (ecMgtA), the phosphorylated aspartate corresponds to Asp 373.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as specific information about ecMgtA.

claim: Phosphorylation induces domain rearrangements leading to the E2P state, which is now open to the periplasmic side.
source: Phosphorylation induces domain rearrangements leading to the E2P state, which is now open to the periplasmic side.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the Post-Albers cycle description.

claim: E2P has low affinity for the bound ions and high affinity for the counter ions.
source: E2P has low affinity for the bound ions and high affinity for the counter ions (Mg2+ in case of MgtA).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the Post-Albers cycle description.

claim: The exchange of counter ions dephosphorylates the enzyme and forms the E2 state.
source: The exchange of counter ions dephosphorylates the enzyme and forms the E2 state.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the Post-Albers cycle description.

claim: Mg2+ is predicted to have high affinity to the E2P state since MgtA imports Mg2+ into the cytoplasm.
source: Since MgtA imports Mg2+ into the cytoplasm, Mg2+ is predicted to have high affinity to the E2P state.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on the transport direction.

claim: The stoichiometry and electrogenic nature of magnesium transport by MgtA remains unknown.
source: However, the stoichiometry and electrogenic nature of magnesium transport by MgtA remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: MgtA was successfully overexpressed in E. coli with yields up to 4 mg per liter of LB medium.
source: In this study, MgtA was successfully overexpressed in its native host E. coli with yields up to 4 mg per liter of LB medium.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental outcome.

claim: Initial affinity purification with His-tag yielded >85% pure protein.
source: Initial affinity purification with His-tag yielded >85% pure protein, additional size exclusion chromatography (SEC) increased the purity up to >95%, resulting in a highly purified protein for in vitro biochemical studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental outcome.

claim: Additional size exclusion chromatography (SEC) increased the purity up to >95%.
source: Initial affinity purification with His-tag yielded >85% pure protein, additional size exclusion chromatography (SEC) increased the purity up to >95%, resulting in a highly purified protein for in vitro biochemical studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental outcome.

claim: A decline in the ATPase activity was observed during purification of wild type MgtA, with more than 90% loss of the ATPase activity after the final SEC purification.
source: A decline in the ATPase activity was observed during purification of wild type (wt) MgtA, with more than 90% loss of the ATPase activity after the final SEC purification (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of total lipid extract from E. coli recovered the ATPase activity of MgtA.
source: Addition of total lipid extract from E. coli recovered the ATPase activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The D373N mutant of MgtA cannot be phosphorylated.
source: We included an inactive mutant (D373N MgtA), which cannot be phosphorylated, as a negative control to rule out the ATPase activity from other endogenous ATPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a characterization of the mutant.

claim: The D373N mutant did not show any significant ATPase activity when supplemented with E. coli lipids.
source: The mutant was purified equivalently to wtMgtA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and did not show any significant ATPase activity when supplemented with E. coli lipids.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phospholipid composition of E. coli inner membrane consists of ~75% phosphatidyl ethanolamine (PE), ~20% phosphatidyl glycerol (PG) and ~5% CL.
source: The phospholipid composition of E. coli inner membrane has been reported to consist of ~75% phosphatidyl ethanolamine (PE), ~20% phosphatidyl glycerol (PG) and ~5% CL (Morein et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Only anionic lipids such as DOPG and E. coli CL restored the ATPase activity in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: To test whether the observed effect of lipids is attributed to a single lipid type, we performed the ATPase assay with increasing amounts of DOPE (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine), DOPG (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol) and CL (isolated from E. coli) and found that only anionic lipids such as DOPG and E. coli CL restored the ATPase activity in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: DOPG activated MgtA by thirty-fold, while CL by hundred-fold, relative to the lipid-free condition.
source: DOPG activated MgtA by thirty-fold, while CL by hundred-fold, relative to the lipid-free condition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: DOPE increased the ATPase activity only by three folds.
source: DOPE increased the ATPase activity only by three folds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: DOPC did not show any measureable effect on the ATPase activity.
source: Further, a non-native E. coli lipid, DOPC (1,2-Dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine), did not show any measureable effect on the ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: E. coli CL has a diverse fatty acid distribution, with 16:0–18:1 as the most dominant (~35%) and 16:0–17:0Δ as the second most dominant (~17%) species.
source: CL isolated from E. coli has a diverse fatty acid distribution, with 16:0–18:1 as the most dominant (~35%) and 16:0–17:0Δ as the second most dominant (~17%) species at positions 1 and 2 of sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (Yokota et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: All four fatty acid chains of bovine heart CL are almost exclusively linoleate chains (18:2, 18:1, 18:3).
source: All the four fatty acid chains of bovine heart CL are almost exclusively linoleate chains (18:2, 18:1, 18:3) (Shinzawa-Itoh et al., 2007; Schlame et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The initial activation profile for both E. coli and bovine heart CL extracts are equivalent.
source: The initial activation profile for both CL extracts are equivalent, which suggest that the head group plays the major role in the activation and not the chemical diversity found within the fatty acid chains in E. coli CL.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: The head group plays the major role in the activation and not the chemical diversity found within the fatty acid chains in E. coli CL.
source: The initial activation profile for both CL extracts are equivalent, which suggest that the head group plays the major role in the activation and not the chemical diversity found within the fatty acid chains in E. coli CL.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of E. coli and bovine heart CL.

claim: The maximal ATPase activity in the presence of bovine heart CL was approximately 30% lower than what was observed with E. coli CL.
source: However, the maximal ATPase activity in the presence of bovine heart CL was approximately 30% lower than what was observed with E. coli CL.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: The longer linoleate chains from bovine heart CL are suboptimal for effective interaction between MgtA and CL.
source: This could mean that the longer linoleate chains from bovine heart CL are suboptimal for effective interaction between MgtA and CL.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the difference in maximal activity.

claim: CL has been shown to bind and facilitate oligomerization in other proteins like the nitrate reductase and SecYEG.
source: Whether MgtA acts as a monomer or dimer in the presence of CL will affect further interpretation of the enzymatic studies since CL has been shown to bind and facilitate oligomerization in other proteins like the nitrate reductase (Arias-Cartin et al., 2011) and SecYEG (Gold et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The SEC elution profile shows a monodisperse peak corresponding to the size of a monomer.
source: The SEC elution profile shows a monodisperse peak corresponding to the size of a monomer (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The SEC profile of MgtA in the presence and absence of CL did not show signs of dimerization of MgtA.
source: The SEC profile of MgtA in the presence and absence of CL did not show signs of dimerization of MgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: A significant shift in the elution peak was observed corresponding to a difference of ~50 kDa when CL was added to MgtA.
source: However, a significant shift in the elution peak was observed corresponding to a difference of ~50 kDa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The shift in elution peak likely indicates an increase in lipid-protein-detergent micelle radius caused by binding of CL to MgtA.
source: This shift likely indicates an increase in lipid-protein-detergent micelle radius caused by binding of CL to MgtA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SEC data.

claim: The presence of Mg2+ with CL does not show any further shift in SEC profile, confirming that MgtA functions as a monomer in the described assay conditions.
source: The presence of Mg2+ with CL does not show any further shift, confirming that MgtA function as a monomer in the described assay conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The general P-type ATPase inhibitor vanadate inhibited the MgtA ATPase activity.
source: The general P-type ATPase inhibitor vanadate as well as specific inhibitors that affect different steps of Post-Albers cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) inhibited the MgtA ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: AlF4- and ADP-AlF4- showed maximal inhibition of MgtA ATPase activity.
source: AlF4- and ADP-AlF4- showed maximal inhibition, followed by vanadate, whereas MgF4- showed only a partial inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MgF4- showed only a partial inhibition of MgtA ATPase activity.
source: AlF4- and ADP-AlF4- showed maximal inhibition, followed by vanadate, whereas MgF4- showed only a partial inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The typical F-type ATPase inhibitor azide had no effect on MgtA ATPase activity.
source: Further, the typical F-type ATPase inhibitor azide had no effect on MgtA ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MgtA behaves like other thoroughly studied P-type ATPase like SERCA.
source: Together these results confirmed that MgtA behaves like other thoroughly studied P-type ATPase like SERCA (Danko et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies with a supporting citation.

claim: Mg2+ transport by MgtA was studied in vivo and reported to show inhibition according to the following order of potency: Zn2+ ≥ Mg2+ > Ni2+ ≈ Co2+ > Ca2+.
source: Mg2+ transport by MgtA was studied in vivo and reported to show inhibition according to the following order of potency: Zn2+ ≥ Mg2+ > Ni2+ ≈ Co2+ > Ca2+ (Snavely et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: In vitro, the order of inhibition of MgtA ATPase activity by divalent ions is Zn2+ > Co2+ > Ni2+ > Ca2+ > Mn2+ > Mg2+.
source: Utilizing our ATPase assay, we investigated the effect of divalent ions in vitro in the presence of CL and 3.0 mM Mg2+ at pH 7.0. We observed the order of inhibition to be Zn2+ > Co2+ > Ni2+ > Ca2+ > Mn2+ > Mg2+ (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: Half maximal inhibition of ATPase activity was found to be at < 5 μM for Zn2+, 37 μM for Co2+, 100 μM for Ni2+, 500 μM for Ca2+ and 1 mM for Mn2+.
source: Half maximal inhibition of ATPase activity was found to be at < 5 μM for Zn2+, 37 μM for Co2+, 100 μM for Ni2+, 500 μM for Ca2+ and 1 mM for Mn2+.

claim: The in vitro inhibition values agree reasonably well with the published in vivo values.
source: These values agree reasonably well with the published values (Snavely et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and published data.

claim: MgtA has been reported to transport Ni2+ as well as Mg2+ and Ni2+ acting as a competitive inhibitor.
source: MgtA has been reported to transport Ni2+ as well as Mg2+ and Ni2+ acting as a competitive inhibitor (Snavely et al., 1991).

claim: Ni2+ likely acts as a non-competitive inhibitor rather than competitive based on ATPase assay data.

claim: CL exists as enriched domains at the poles and division septa in E. coli.

source: NAO is widely used to image anionic phospholipids in bacteria and displays a specific red-shifted fluorescence emission when bound to CL (Mileykovskaya et al., 2001).

source: The confocal images of MgtA (gene locus: JW4201) fused to GFP from GenoBase showed clear fluorescence localized at the poles.

claim: Confocal images of E. coli C43(DE3) overexpressing MgtA-BFP confirmed that it was mainly concentrated at the poles and colocalized with the NAO-stained CL domains.
source: The confocal images of E. coli C43(DE3) overexpressing MgtA-BFP confirmed that it was mainly concentrated at the poles and colocalized with the NAO-stained CL domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 3A.

claim: The NΔ31-MgtA-BFP was also found at the poles and colocalized with CL.
source: The NΔ31-MgtA-BFP was also found at the poles and colocalized with CL (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 3B.

claim: The overexpressed BFP alone did not colocalize with the NAO stained CL.
source: As a control, the overexpressed BFP alone did not colocalize with the NAO stained CL (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 3C.

claim: No significant difference in the ATPase activity between the purified wt and NΔ31 mutant was observed.
source: Furthermore, no significant difference in the ATPase activity between the purified wt and NΔ31 mutant (Figure 3D) was observed.

claim: The intrinsic disorder predicted in the N-termini of both MgtA in E. coli and MgtA/B in S. typhimurium is not required for activation by lipids.
source: This suggests that unlike ATP13A2, the intrinsic disorder predicted in the N-termini of both MgtA in E. coli and MgtA/B in S. typhimurium is not required for activation by lipids and do not play any role in membrane trafficking or targeting to the CL domains (Figure 3E).

claim: The intrinsic disorder predicted in the N-termini of MgtA does not play any role in membrane trafficking or targeting to the CL domains.
source: This suggests that unlike ATP13A2, the intrinsic disorder predicted in the N-termini of both MgtA in E. coli and MgtA/B in S. typhimurium is not required for activation by lipids and do not play any role in membrane trafficking or targeting to the CL domains (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NΔ31 mutant studies.

claim: The nonphosphorylable mutant D373N fused to GFP showed similar localization at the poles.

claim: The active transport of ions through MgtA does not affect trafficking to the membrane or its localization in the membrane.
source: This leads us to conclude that the active transport of ions through MgtA does not affect trafficking to the membrane or its localization in the membrane.

source: The ATPase activity was measured at three fixed concentrations (1.0, 3.0 and 6.0 mM) of ATP, with increasing concentrations of Mg2+ (Mg2+total) from 0 to 10.0 mM.

claim: The activation profile was slightly shifted towards higher Mg2+total as the ATP concentration in assay buffer increased.
source: However, the activation profile was slightly shifted towards higher Mg2+total as the ATP concentration in assay buffer increased.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The activating concentration of Mg2+free was equivalent (~10.0 μM) for all three fixed ATP concentrations.
source: We found that the activating concentration of Mg2+free was equivalent (~10.0 μM) for all three fixed ATP concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The ATPase activity peaked at 250 μM Mg2+free and was inhibited rapidly above 1.0 mM Mg2+free.
source: Further, we observed that the ATPase activity peaked at 250 μM Mg2+free and was inhibited rapidly above 1.0 mM Mg2+free.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The cytoplasmic Mg2+free concentration is ~1 mM.
source: Since the cytoplasmic Mg2+free concentration is ~1 mM (Silver and Clark, 1971; Froschauer et al., 2004), the inhibition that is observed could occur from the cytoplasmic side of MgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The apparent Km for Mg2+free is between 10–15 μM for the three ATP concentrations tested.
source: We also calculated the apparent Km for Mg2+free to be between 10–15 μM for the three ATP concentrations tested (Figure 4C, Table 1) which is only slightly lower than the reported ~29 μM from in vivo studies with S. typhimurium at 37°C (Snavely et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: The apparent Km for Mg2+free is only slightly lower than the reported ~29 μM from in vivo studies with S. typhimurium at 37°C.
source: We also calculated the apparent Km for Mg2+free to be between 10–15 μM for the three ATP concentrations tested (Figure 4C, Table 1) which is only slightly lower than the reported ~29 μM from in vivo studies with S. typhimurium at 37°C (Snavely et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and published data.

claim: The ATPase activity peaked when the molar concentration of ATP was equivalent to the indicated levels of molar Mg2+total in the complementary experiment with increasing ATP concentrations.
source: Correspondingly in a complementary experiment, the ATPase activity was measured at six fixed Mg2+total concentrations with increasing ATP concentrations from 0–10.0 mM (Figure 4D). As observed in Figure 4A, the ATPase activity peaked when the molar concentration of ATP was equivalent to the indicated levels of molar Mg2+total.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: A slight decrease in the ATPase activity was observed at higher concentrations of ATP for all fixed Mg2+total.
source: However, a slight decrease in the ATPase activity was observed at higher concentrations of ATP for all fixed Mg2+total.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: ATPfree is competing for the Mg2+-ATP binding site, thereby reducing the MgtA-Mg2+-ATP complex formation.
source: This could indicate that the ATPfree is competing for the Mg2+-ATP binding site, thereby reducing the MgtA-Mg2+-ATP complex formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the decrease in activity at high ATP concentrations.

claim: Maximum ATPase activity was observed at pH 7.2.
source: To check the influence of pH on MgtA, we tested the MgtA Mg2+total dependency at different pH values (Figure 4E). Maximum ATPase activity was observed at pH 7.2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: At all pH values, a decrease in ATPase activity at higher Mg2+total concentration was observed corresponding to product inhibition.
source: However, at all pH values, a decrease in ATPase activity at higher Mg2+total concentration was observed corresponding to product inhibition as seen in Figure 4A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: In the pH range from 6.3 to 7.2, the activation and inhibition profiles were equivalent with only decrease in the maximum ATPase activity when the pH is below 7.0.
source: When the ATPase activity was plotted against Mg2+free (Figure 4F), it became clear that in the pH range from 6.3 to 7.2, the activation and inhibition profiles were equivalent with only decrease in the maximum ATPase activity when the pH is below 7.0.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: At pH 7.6 and pH 7.9, the affinity for Mg2+free was reduced, but the inhibition by Mg2+free was equivalent to the other pH ranges.
source: At pH 7.6 and pH 7.9, the affinity for Mg2+free was reduced, but the inhibition by Mg2+free was equivalent to the other pH ranges.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: The data do not show any clear proton dependent Mg2+ affinity for MgtA.
source: Our data do not show any clear proton dependent Mg2+ affinity for MgtA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pH dependency studies.

claim: The MgtA homolog PH1 from P. hybrida did not show proton transport activity.
source: Considering that the MgtA homolog PH1 from P. hybrida did not show proton transport activity (Faraco et al., 2014), we have to question whether proton counter transport occurs in MgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Both MgtA and PH lack the membrane imbedded arginine, which is important for proton translocation as described for the P3A-type (H+) ATPases.
source: Both MgtA and PH lack the membrane imbedded arginine, which is important for proton translocation as described for the P3A-type (H+) ATPases, Pma1 (Arg 695) in yeast (Dutra et al., 1998) and AHA2 (Arg 655) in Arabidopsis (Buch-Pedersen and Palmgren, 2003; Pedersen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: MgtA may be importing magnesium without the need for proton as counter ion.
source: These observations suggest that MgtA may be importing magnesium without the need for proton as counter ion.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the lack of proton dependency and the absence of key arginine residue.

claim: The pH dependent ATPase activity changes may not be linked to proton translocation.
source: Since enzymatic activity in general is affected by changes in pH, the pH dependent ATPase activity changes we observe may not be linked to proton translocation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pH dependency data.

claim: The role of protons as counterions for MgtA awaits further verification.
source: The role of protons as counterions for MgtA therefore awaits further verification.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the uncertainty regarding proton counter transport.

claim: The purification process decreased the ATPase activity of MgtA, indicating the removal of an activating compound or an interacting partner.
source: Towards the aim of enzymatic characterization of MgtA, we purified MgtA and demonstrated the tight association of MgtA with CL, and sensitivity of MgtA towards Mg2+, providing the first step in understanding the P3B-type ATPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: The results are the first to link activation by CL to any P-type ATPase.
source: Our results are the first to link activation by CL to any P-type ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding.

claim: CL has often been linked to membrane proteins connected with the oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and membrane proteins involved with lipid metabolism.
source: CL has often been linked to membrane proteins connected with the oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and membrane proteins involved with lipid metabolism (Planas-Iglesias et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: MgtA does not exhibit oligomerization in presence of CL or CL-Mg2+ in vitro.
source: MgtA does not exhibit oligomerization in presence of CL or CL-Mg2+ in vitro
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the SEC data.

claim: CL likely causes a small structural change directly on the protein surface either by binding to a specific site or by facilitating Mg2+free recognition.
source: Thus, CL likely causes a small structural change directly on the protein surface either by binding to a specific site or by facilitating Mg2+free recognition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The CL binding does not occur at the N-terminus.
source: Our data suggests that the CL binding does not occur at the N-terminus but at an yet unidentified site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the NΔ31 mutant data.

claim: The preferential selection of CL in the presence of other lipid types hints that MgtA function may be regulated in vivo by changing the local concentration of CL.
source: The preferential selection of CL in the presence of other lipid types hint that MgtA function may be regulated in vivo by changing the local concentration of CL.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: CL forms domains or rafts at the poles and division septa in E. coli.
source: Since CL have been shown to form domains or rafts at the poles and division septa in E. coli (Renner and Weibel, 2011), we hypothesized that MgtA could be localized in these CL domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A recent study questions the specificity of NAO to CL, and shows that NAO stains both anionic phospholipids, PG and CL in the membrane and at the poles of E. coli.
source: However, a recent study questions the specificity of NAO to CL, and shows that NAO stains both anionic phospholipids, PG and CL in the membrane and at the poles of E. coli (Oliver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: It is not possible to distinguish which anionic lipid among CL and PG would have the most pronounced effect on MgtA in vivo in the E. coli inner membrane considering the discrepancies in NAO staining.
source: Considering the discrepancies in NAO staining, it is not possible to distinguish which anionic lipid among CL and PG would have the most pronounced effect on MgtA in vivoin the E. coli inner membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the NAO staining method.

claim: Expression of MgtA and consequent removal of Mg2+ from the periplasm by MgtA further activated the sensor kinase PhoQ of the two-component system PhoQ/PhoP.
source: It has earlier been reported that expression of MgtA and consequent removal of Mg2+ from the periplasm by MgtA further activated the sensor kinase PhoQ of the two-component system PhoQ/PhoP. This positive feedback regulation increased the level phosphorylated PhoP, which is necessary for the expression of subset of genes expressed under low Mg2+ condition Park and Groisman, 2014
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation (note: citation formatting appears incomplete in source).

claim: PhoP of the two-component system PhoQ/P goes to one pole in S. typhimurium when activated by phosphorylation.
source: It is interesting to note that PhoP of the two-component system PhoQ/P, which activates MgtA expression, also goes to one pole in S. typhimurium when activated by phosphorylation (Sciara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The localization of MgtA in CL rich domains in the poles connects the localization observed for activated PhoP and MgtA.
source: Our observation that MgtA is localized in CL rich domains in the poles, thus connect the localization observed for activated PhoP and MgtA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The exact molecular mechanism behind the similar localization pattern of MgtA-CL and PhoP remains to be determined.
source: However the exact molecular mechanism behind the similar localization pattern of MgtA-CL and PhoP remains to be determined.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a knowledge gap.

claim: Activation by both anionic lipids has been observed for other membrane proteins, including the anaerobic respiratory complex in E. coli, the mechanosensitive channel MscL, the protein translocon complex SecYEG and the cell division proteins MinD and MinE.
source: Activation by both anionic lipids has been observed for other membrane proteins, including the anaerobic respiratory complex in E. coli (Arias-Cartin et al., 2011), the mechanosensitive channel MscL (Powl et al., 2003), the protein translocon complex SecYEG (Gold et al., 2010) and the cell division proteins MinD and MinE (Renner and Weibel, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: It is reasonable to conclude that MgtA is active in an anionic phospholipid environment.
source: Thus, it is reasonable to conclude that MgtA is active in an anionic phospholipid environment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: In bacteria, CL is synthesized by the fusion of two PG molecules.
source: In bacteria, CL is synthesized by the fusion of two PG molecules (Tropp, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: CL carries two negative charges in the head group, while PG carries only one.
source: While CL carries two negative charges in the head group, PG carries only one.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: The difference in charge between CL and PG could contribute either to efficient binding of lipid or efficient presentation of substrate (Mg2+) to MgtA.
source: This difference in the charge could contribute either to efficient binding of lipid or efficient presentation of substrate (Mg2+) to MgtA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: CL can bind divalent cations like Mg2+ and undergo lipid phase changes as a function of Mg2+ concentration.
source: It has been shown that CL can bind divalent cations like Mg2+ and undergo lipid phase changes as a function of Mg2+ concentration(Vail and Stollery, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: CL could act as a Mg2+ reservoir or as a chaperone for easy substrate presentation to MgtA.
source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that CL could act as a Mg2+ reservoir or as a chaperone for easy substrate presentation to MgtA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Cu+-ATPases from the P1B-type ATPase family require protein chaperones that are either part of the Cu+-ATPases or expressed as separate proteins in cytoplasm to bind and deliver Cu+ to the Cu+-ATPases.
source: The Cu+-ATPases from the P1B-type ATPase family are well known to require protein chaperones that are either part of the Cu+-ATPases or expressed as separate proteins in cytoplasm to bind and deliver Cu+ to the Cu+-ATPases (Arguello et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The head group of cardiolipin could function as the Mg2+ chaperone for MgtA.
source: This, it is intriguing to speculate that the head group of CL could function as the Mg2+ chaperone for MgtA and its function could differ depending on the side it associates with MgtA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: A crystal structure of CL bound to MgtA will be necessary to determine the sidedness of the CL headgroup binding site in MgtA.
source: However to further address these questions, a crystal structure of CL bound to MgtA will be necessary as it is not possible to determine the sidedness of the CL headgroup binding site in MgtA in the present study.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future direction.

claim: MgtA is activated already below 10 μM Mg2+free.
source: Surprisingly, the effect of Mg2+ on the ATPase activity of MgtA was more pronounced than expected. MgtA is activated already below 10 μM Mg2+free.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: MgtA is highly sensitive to the Mg2+free and the level of sensitivity is different from other P-type ATPases.
source: Even though our data does not conclusively establish the transport of Mg2+ by MgtA, it shows that MgtA is highly sensitive to the Mg2+free and the level of sensitivity is different from other P-type ATPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The related H+ ATPase from Neurospora crassa shows decrease in ATPase activity at higher Mg2+ concentration but is not completely inhibited even above 20 mM of Mg2+total.
source: The related H+ ATPase from Neurospora crassa also shows decrease in ATPase activity at higher Mg2+ concentration (Brooker and Slayman, 1983). However, it is not completely inhibited even above 20 mM of Mg2+total, whereas MgtA is completely inhibited above 5 mM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: MgtA is completely inhibited above 5 mM Mg2+total.
source: The related H+ ATPase from Neurospora crassa also shows decrease in ATPase activity at higher Mg2+ concentration (Brooker and Slayman, 1983). However, it is not completely inhibited even above 20 mM of Mg2+total, whereas MgtA is completely inhibited above 5 mM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: MgtA presents a strikingly narrow activity range induced by Mg2+ as compared to the H+ ATPase.
source: MgtA presents a strikingly narrow activity range induced by Mg2+ as compared to the H+ ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison.

claim: MgtA is more sensitive to Mg2+ concentrations in vitro than any other studied P-type ATPase.
source: Overall, we conclude that MgtA is more sensitive to Mg2+ concentrations in vitro than any other studied P-type ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The sensitivity towards Mg2+ points out that Mg2+ is the ion transported through MgtA in vivo.
source: This sensitivity towards Mg2+ points out that Mg2+ is the ion transported through MgtA in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference.

claim: The narrow activity range suggests that MgtA could have more Mg2+ binding sites other than the transport sites to sense the varying Mg2+free concentrations.
source: The narrow activity range suggests that MgtA could have more Mg2+ binding sites other than the transport sites to sense the varying Mg2+free concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The Mg2+free concentration of E. coli and S. enterica cytoplasms is found to be ~1 mM.
source: The Mg2+free concentration of E. coli and S. enterica cytoplasms is found to be ~1 mM (Silver and Clark, 1971; Froschauer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The observation that MgtA transports Mg2+ into the cytoplasm and its ATPase activity decreases above the physiological 1 mM Mg2+free strengthens the notion that the cytoplasmic Mg2+free concentration also regulates MgtA internally.
source: The observation that MgtA transports Mg2+ into the cytoplasm and its ATPase activity decreases above the physiological 1 mM Mg2+free, strengthens the notion that the cytoplasmic Mg2+free concentration also regulates MgtA internally.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: Increasing cytoplasmic Mg2+ concentrations negatively regulates mgtA-coding region.
source: Additionally, it has been reported that increasing cytoplasmic Mg2+ concentrations negatively regulates mgtA-coding region (Cromie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: When the Mg2+ concentration in the cytoplasm exceeds the threshold, Mg2+free negatively regulates both MgtA in PG-CL domain and mgtA coding region.
source: When the Mg2+ concentration in the cytoplasm exceeds the threshold, Mg2+free negatively regulates both MgtA in PG-CL domain and mgtA coding region (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and illustrated in Figure 5 as part of the proposed model.

claim: The data supports that MgtA acts both as a transporter and as a sensor for Mg2+.
source: In conclusion, our data supports that MgtA acts both as a transporter and as asensor for Mg2+.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as the main conclusion.
